blocks.text: An equilibrium in which the reactants and products are in more than one phases is called heterogeneous equilibrium. The following are examples of heterogeneous equilibrium:
highlight: An equilibrium in which the reactants and products are in more than one phases is called heterogeneous equilibrium.

blocks.prompt: a) Differentiate between homogeneous and heterogeneous equilibria
blocks.explanation: The differences are given in the table.

rows: All reactants and products are in the same phase
Reactants and products are in more than one phase
Examples: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) (all gases), formation of an ester (all liquids)
Example: CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g) (solids and a gas)
The concentrations of all species appear in the equilibrium constant
Pure solids and pure liquids do not appear in the expression, e.g. Kc = [CO₂]

blocks.prompt: b) Why do the rates of forward reactions slow down when a reversible reaction approaches the equilibrium stage?
blocks.explanation: The forward rate depends on the concentration of the reactants. As reactants are converted into products, there are fewer collisions every second and the forward rate falls. At the same time the products build up and the reverse rate rises, until at equilibrium the two rates are equal.

blocks.prompt:
c) In soda water bottles, gaseous CO₂ is in equilibrium with the aqueous CO₂ (HCO₃⁻ and H⁺).
i. Condition for this equilibrium requires the closed cap of the bottle. Why?
ii. When the cap of the bottle is removed, to which direction the equilibrium shifts?
blocks.explanation: (i) With the cap closed, the CO₂ that escapes from the water stays inside the bottle and dissolves again at the same rate; the system is closed, so the equilibrium is kept. (ii) When the cap is removed, CO₂ gas escapes, so the equilibrium shifts to the left (towards the reactants): dissolved CO₂ keeps coming out as bubbles and the soda goes flat.
